newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai firms avoid contracts, face disputes.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai firms avoid contracts, face disputes.

text.p: Most state-run companies in China's commercial centre of Shanghai don't bother to sign contracts in their business deals, making disputes hard to resolve, an official newspaper said on Tuesday.
A survey of some 70 Shanghai companies showed that contracts played a minor role in business deals, particularly for state-run companies, the Business News said.

Only 12.93 percent of the state-owned enterprises surveyed signed contracts when doing business, while private companies and foreign joint ventures showed much higher ratios of 68 percent and 74 percent.
State firms preferred to deal with long-time customers with a promise, or demanded cash payments from newer clients.
"The low use of contracts will make production of these state enterprises difficult to manage," an official in charge of the survey was quoted as saying.
He added that the reliance on cash payments tied up working capital of local companies while the lack of a contract meant the legal system was often unable to resolve disputes.
"In the event of a dispute, these state-owned companies face major problems," he said.
China's shift towards a market economy from its old Stalinist central planning has created a growing need to boost the legal system, requiring the training of lawyers and judges.
Lawyers say, however, that enforcement of laws is still lagging and many companies may choose to resolve disputes themselves without turning to the court system.
